extracted.intended_audience: zoologists, taxonomists, museum staff, and advanced students of invertebrate zoology
extracted.subtask_description: Identification and systematic description of freshwater sponges (family Spongillidae / Spongillidæ) based on morphology, skeleton and spicule characters, life-history features (gemmules, reproduction), and ecological/variation notes. Intended to guide species recognition, description, and comparison of Indian freshwater sponges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phylum Porifera diagnostic features
rubrics_metrics.description: Members distinguished from compound Protozoa by cells that exhibit considerable differentiation and are associated together though not forming organs or systems; digestion performed entirely by individual cells; presence of pores and an osculum; collar-cells (choanocytes) lining the interior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key diagnostic traits listed include: multicellular organization with differentiated cells but no organs or nervous system; internal collar-cells with a rim or collar and a central flagellum; pores (inhalent apertures) and osculum (exhalent aperture). The simple olynthus (hollow vase-like body) is noted as the simplest form. Footnote: collar-cells are practically identical with those of Choanoflagellata.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collar-cells (choanocytes) structure and role
rubrics_metrics.description: Collar-cells consist of a rim/collar of membrane surrounding a central flagellum; they form the gastral layer and produce the water-currents that drive feeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collar-cells are minute and extremely numerous; their flagella set up water-currents that draw food into the sponge, and they select and engulf fine organic particles. Fig. 2D and high-power microscopy are required to examine them (very high magnification cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cellular diversity and plasticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Sponges contain various cell kinds in a gelatinous matrix, many of which can move amoeboidally and change form and function (including membrane cells, gastral cells, glandular cells, reproductive cells).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some cells give rise to spicules or spongin; any one kind of cell may change function and form if needed. Recognize glandular vs amoeboid vs non-amoeboid cells; note special 'bubble-cells' in some genera.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skeleton composition (spongin vs spicules; calcareous vs siliceous)
rubrics_metrics.description: Skeletons may be horny (spongin), calcareous, or siliceous; in Demospongiæ (including Spongillidæ) spicules (when present) are typically siliceous (opal) and spongin may be present binding spicules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chemical nature of spicules (lime salts vs silica) is important for classification. Note some sponges have mixed spicule types. Amount of spongin affects consistency and appearance. Historically classification used these distinctions; modern system may be more complex but composition remains diagnostic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spicule types: megascleres and microscleres
rubrics_metrics.description: Larger skeleton-spicules (megascleres) are rod- or needle-like, usually with one main axis; smaller free spicules (microscleres or flesh-spicules) are variable in form and often lie loose in the substance and membrane or form armature of gemmules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Megascleres typically form reticulate skeleton fibres; microscleres vary in size and shape and are critical for species/genus recognition. Examine both skeleton-spicules and free spicules for identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spicule morphology and ornamentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Normal spicules are rod-like or needle-like, blunt or pointed at both ends, and may be smooth, granular, or covered with small spines. Some free spicules have complex forms (e.g., several shafts meeting at a central nodule, recurved hooks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for characteristic forms: double grappling-iron shapes in Corvospongilla, comb-like rows of spines in Pectispongilla, disks on gemmule-spicules, etc. Surface ornamentation (smooth, granular, spiny) is diagnostic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gemmule-spicules and gemmule structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Gemmule-spicules almost always present in mature gemmules in Spongillidæ and are of great importance in distinguishing genera; they may resemble free microscleres or bear transverse disks or comb-like spines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine gemmule armature closely when present — disked or spined terminations are genus-level characters. Gemmule morphology is emphasized as a primary systematic character for the family.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spicule microstructure (organic filament within silica)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each spicule, though mainly hydrated silica (opal), contains a slender organic filament running along its main axis inside the silica; in some species the filament's termination is marked by minute conical protuberances at both ends of the megasclere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note internal organic filament when examining spicules under very high magnification; such micro-features may aid species-level identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrangement of spicules into skeleton fibres
rubrics_metrics.description: In reticulate skeletons spicules form fibres of two kinds: radiating fibres (radiate from sponge centre, often penetrate external membrane) and transverse fibres (run across between radiating fibres). Fibres are composed of large spicules arranged parallel and bound by spongin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish radiating vs transverse fibres when assessing skeletal architecture. Radiating fibres often form tent-like elevations of membrane; transverse fibres may be single spicules or hour-glass shaped in outline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free spicules distribution and significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Free spicules, when present, are usually needle-like and pointed, sometimes variable in form; they may be absent in many species but when present they are systematically important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspect both substance and dermal membrane for loose spicules; their presence/absence and form inform genus/species decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inhalent apertures / porocyte structure and variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Inhalent apertures vary: in some species pores are spaces between flattened cells; in others each pore pierces a ring-shaped porocyte; occasionally pores are enclosed by two crescent-shaped cells. Porocytes may occur below the derma or at chamber entrances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Porocyte presence and form differ even among close species; some authors dispute porocytes in Demospongiae. Practical note: porocytes are difficult to see in thin sections — a fragment of membrane must be mounted whole (Footnote M). Compare species examples: Spongilla carteri vs S. proliferens, S. crassissima.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oscular form and oscular collar
rubrics_metrics.description: The external membrane often forms an oscular collar around oscula; the collar is highly contractile but cannot fully close; form of oscula (size, stellate margins, raised crater-like) is characteristic of many species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use oscular shape and collar prominence as species characters — e.g., Spongilla carteri has very large, well-defined oscula; some species have stellate oscula due to grooves radiating beneath membrane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bubble-cells as a diagnostic cell-type
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Bubble-cells' are comparatively large spherical cells containing a central globule of liquid, characteristic of some species (e.g., some Ephydatia) and distinguishable from porocytes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize bubble-cells by optical appearance (globule forcing protoplasm to a delicate film). Their presence is a diagnostic trait for certain genera.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colour and odour as diagnostic characters (and their causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Freshwater sponges commonly have a bad odour (probably protective); colour is usually dull and uniform but may be bright (e.g., Pectispongilla aurea) or green from 'green corpuscles'. Colours arise from inhalation of inorganic particles, pigments produced by sponge, or presence of green corpuscles (likely algal). Parasitic algae can also colour dying sponges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret colour cautiously: it may reflect ingested silt, metabolic pigments, symbiotic algae, or parasitic algae in dying individuals. Odour is noted but function is uncertain. Conduct simple experiments (e.g., carmine uptake) to test ingestion/elimination of particles.

rubrics_metrics.name: External form and surface characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Each species/subspecies/variety has a characteristic external appearance (branching, flattened branches, lichenoid cushions, turret-like projections, smooth spherical forms); oscula, ridges, and surface projections are often species-specific.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use habit (branching vs cushion), surface ornamentation (ridges, turret-like projections), and tendency to anastomose as field-identification characters. Note that tropical freshwater sponges less often produce long branches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency (firmness) and its causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Consistency ranges from almost stony to soft and compressible; determined by number of spicules and amount of spongin. Examples: Corvospongilla lapidosa and Spongilla crassissima are very hard/stony, while Spongilla lacustris var. mollis is soft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess consistency as an identification trait and relate to spicule density/arrangement and spongin abundance. Hardness may reflect interlocking spicules with little spongin or a profuse spongin matrix binding a reticulate skeleton.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation to consider in identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Sponges exhibit considerable variation: (a) seasonal variation (cell numbers and anatomy may change), (b) environmentally-induced variation (form and colour change with currents, substrate, water quality), and (c) variation without apparent cause; spicule size/shape may vary too.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When naming/separating species, account for intra-species variation due to season, environment, or unexplained causes; examine multiple specimens and contexts. The author gives locality and season examples showing morphological plasticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nutrition and feeding behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Food taken in by water currents produced by collar-cell flagella; collar-cells and probably other cells select and engulf suitable particles; some sponges ingest milk and can absorb dissolved material. Green corpuscles (symbiotic algae) may provide nourishment via photosynthesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand feeding mode when interpreting pigment and colouration; experimental observations (e.g., carmine uptake) demonstrate capacity to ingest and later eliminate particulate matter. Consider potential contribution of symbiotic green corpuscles to nutrition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproductive modes and their taxonomic importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Spongillidæ reproduce by eggs, buds (rarely), and gemmules; gemmules are elaborated and of special systematic importance. Most species are potentially monoecious; fertilization may be self or cross.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gemmule morphology (including gemmule-spicules) is emphasized for genus/species separation. Note frequency of budding in species like Spongilla proliferens where sexual reproduction may be rare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canal system anatomy and water flow pathways
rubrics_metrics.description: Water enters through pores into a subdermal cavity, is forced into inhalent canals and ciliated chambers, then into exhalent canals and out via oscula; increased complexity reduces the simple olynthus and often produces multiple oscula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map canal architecture (presence/size of subdermal cavity, canal complexity, chamber arrangement, number of oscula) when comparing species; diagrams (fig.1) and microanatomy (ciliated chambers) are useful guides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical observation recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain structures require specific preparation to be seen: porocytes are difficult in thin microtome sections and require whole mounted membrane fragments; very high-power microscopy is necessary for collar-cells and spicule microstructure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mount membrane fragments whole for porocyte observation (Footnote M); use sufficient magnification and good preservation/staining to view collar-cells and gemmule-spicule development (see fig.2 and fig.2E). Consult referenced works (Minchin, Sollas, Weltner) for more technical methods.
